Trauma, Stress and Dissociative Disorders

acute stress disorder · posttraumatic stress disorder · adjustment disorder · dissociative disordersTrauma or stressor, and how long since?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Trauma (actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violation), then intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal 3 days to 1 month after the trauma: acute stress disorder; over 1 month: posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
  • A non-traumatic stressor with outsized distress within 3 months of the stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends, short of another disorder (in the depressed-mood type, fewer than 5 depressive symptoms) adjustment disorder; lost personal memory with negative toxicology and no neurologic cause dissociative amnesia, with fugue if the patient travels
  • Trauma-focused CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) first; for PTSD an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or an SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) is also first line; prazosin for nightmares that persist
What it is

Disorders that follow a trauma or a stressor, and dissociative disorders: disrupted memory, identity or sense of reality, often after trauma

Driver

A trauma raised norepinephrine and reduced serotonin activity: a heightened sympathetic response

Triggers

Severe trauma, such as major injury or prolonged exposure

Trauma to oneself rather than witnessed

Previous trauma; abuse or neglect in childhood non-modifiable

Dissociation during the trauma

Limited social support

A psychiatric disorder before the trauma non-modifiable

Chain

Event: a trauma adrenergic surge: startle, fast heart rate

Reaction: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, arousal, dissociation acute stress disorder, 3 days to 1 month after the trauma

Course: symptoms over 1 month the diagnosis changes to PTSD; 40% to 80% progress

Insights

Dissociation inside an acute stress or PTSD picture earns no separate dissociative diagnosis; intrusion, avoidance and arousal should be there too

Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors, so it damps the adrenergic hyperactivity behind PTSD nightmares

Comorbidity and populationtap to open
ComorbidCommon with PTSD: screen for and treat themMajor depressive disorder, bipolar disorder and substance use disorders; when depression criteria are also met, diagnose both
SexPTSD is more common in womenDissociative identity disorder is also more common in women
ChildrenPTSD can start as young as age 1Young children may have nightmares not specific to the trauma, and replay its themes in play
Sexual assaultRaises the risk of PTSD, depression and suicidality
2Urgent risks
SuicideAcute stress disorder and PTSD raise suicide risk; most patients with dissociative identity disorder attempt suicide

If a patient has an acute stress, posttraumatic or dissociative disorder, choose screening for suicidal ideation and a safety plan.

Returning memoryRisk rises as dissociative amnesia lifts and memories return

If memory is coming back in dissociative amnesia, choose screening for suicidal ideation and self-injury.

3Differential
After a trauma or stressor: look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Low mood, poor sleep and focus after a loss5 or more symptoms for 2 weeks or more; fewer after a stressor is adjustment disorder; sad mood, poor sleep and poor focus in response to a trauma belong to the trauma disorder; when full criteria for both are met, diagnose both
Waking with palpitations, sweating and breathlessnessRecurrent, unexpected attacks; attacks likely set off by trauma dreams are not panic disorder
Tension, insomnia, poor focusWorry about many everyday matters for 6 months or more, not tied to one event
Clinging fear of being leftA lifelong pattern; anxiety that began weeks ago, after a stressor, is not a personality disorder
Hallucinations or delusions, often after a stressorResolves within a month; psychosis is not part of acute stress disorder
A defiant, aggressive childWith trauma, nightmares and avoidance, the aggression is PTSD arousal
Dissociation: medical and substance causes first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Substance blackout or intoxicationA memory gap after alcohol or drugsToxicology or the history finds the substance; rule it out before any dissociative diagnosis
Transient global amnesiaSudden loss of new memoriesIdentity kept; the loss is anterograde, for time and place
Dissociative amnesia, with fugue if the patient travelsLost identity or personal history after a stressor; may wanderAutobiographical memory lost, other cognition intact; no substance or neurologic cause
Depersonalization/derealization disorderDetached from self or surroundingsMemory and reality testing intact
Dissociative identity disorderMemory gaps; may find belongings with no memory of owning them2 or more distinct identities take turns in control
Acute stress disorder or PTSDDissociation after a traumaIntrusion, avoidance and arousal as well: no separate dissociative diagnosis
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
A trauma 2 weeks ago; nightmares, startle, feels in a daze, will not talk about itAcute stress disorderStart trauma-focused CBT, as in step 7
Neglect years ago; nightmares, avoidance and aggression in a childPTSD, not oppositional defiant disorderTreat as PTSD, as in step 7
A breakup or job loss weeks ago; restless or tearful, short of another disorderAdjustment disorderStart brief supportive psychotherapy, as in step 7
Found far from home, cannot say who they are, after a deathDissociative amnesia with fugueOrder toxicology and a neurologic check first, as in First step
Flashbacks gone on an SSRI and CBT, but bad dreams continuePersistent PTSD nightmaresAdd prazosin, as in step 7
Pause point
Burned 3 weeks ago; nightmares, startle, sad and tearful Offered as PTSD or major depression Still within 1 month of the trauma → Acute stress disorder
Tearful, poor appetite and focus a month after a partner's affair Offered as major depressive episode Fewer than 5 symptoms, after a stressor → Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
Restless and anxious 2 weeks after a breakup Offered as acute stress disorder or generalized anxiety disorder No life-threatening event; far short of 6 months of worry → Adjustment disorder with anxiety
Aggressive foster child with nightmares, hiding and school refusal Offered as oppositional defiant disorder or separation anxiety Neglect years ago; symptoms over 1 month → PTSD
5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: acute stress disorder and PTSD Event – actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violation · Symptoms – intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal; acute stress disorder counts dissociation too and needs 9 or more symptoms · Clock – acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month after the trauma; PTSD over 1 month, with distress or impaired function · Test – none; the diagnosis is clinical
Defining criteria: adjustment disorder Stressor – identifiable and not life-threatening · Response – distress out of proportion to the stressor, with significant functional impairment · Clock – within 3 months of the stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends · Exclusion – another disorder's criteria not met; the depressed-mood type has fewer than 5 depressive symptoms · Types – with anxiety, with depressed mood, or with conduct disturbance
Defining criteria: dissociative disorders Dissociative amnesia – cannot recall important personal information, usually about a trauma or stress; with fugue when the patient travels or wanders · Depersonalization/derealization disorder – persistent or recurrent detachment from self or surroundings; reality testing intact · Dissociative identity disorder – 2 or more distinct identities that alternate in control, with memory gaps · All – not from a substance or a medical condition such as seizures, and not better explained by acute stress disorder or PTSD
7Treatment

Acute stress disorder and PTSD

1

First lineAcute stress disorder or PTSD

Trauma-focused CBT

Start early in acute stress disorder, which raises the risk of PTSD; pharmacotherapy is typically not indicated there. For PTSD, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing is another trauma-focused therapy

2

First line, PTSDWith or instead of therapy; may also be first line when therapy is declined or unavailable, or depression or anxiety coexists

An SSRI or SNRI

Preferred for tolerability and efficacy; once it works, keep it: tapering risks relapse, and switching could worsen other PTSD symptoms

3

AdjunctNightmares persist on an SSRI or SNRI

Add prazosin at bedtime

Titrate to avoid orthostatic hypotension; a benzodiazepine does not help the nightmares and risks dependence Psychotherapy optionImage rehearsal therapy rewrites the nightmare with a better ending

Other disorders: first treatment
DisorderChooseWatch for
Adjustment disorderBrief supportive psychotherapy; a short course of a drug for a target symptom may be addedTypically self-limited
Dissociative amnesiaA supportive environment; memory may return on its ownSuicidal ideation and self-injury as memory returns, as in step 2
Depersonalization/derealization disorderReassurance, then CBT for grounding skillsFear of going crazy
Dissociative identity disorderTrauma-focused psychotherapy aimed at integrating the identitiesMost attempt suicide, as in step 2
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo or expect
Acute stress disorder, at 1 monthReassess: symptoms over 1 month mean PTSD; 40% to 80% progress
Adjustment disorderExpect it gone within 6 months after the stressor ends
PTSD, over yearsOften chronic: about a third recover within a year; a third still have symptoms at 10 years
Practice
  1. 35-year-old man seen 2 weeks after a highway crash that killed the other driver wakes from dreams of the crash; jumps at car horns feels unreal, as if watching himself; will not drive no drug use; examination normal → Acute stress disorder → a trauma, then intrusion, arousal, avoidance and dissociation 2 weeks later: acute stress disorder, 3 days to 1 month after the trauma; PTSD needs symptoms over 1 month, and dissociation inside an acute stress picture is not a separate disorder
  2. 9-year-old girl brought by her grandmother, who gained custody 2 years ago as a toddler she was left alone for days without food or heat nightmares, startles easily, hits classmates, will not sleep alone growth and examination normal → Posttraumatic stress disorder → severe neglect, then nightmares, startle, aggression and avoidance far longer than 1 month: PTSD; with trauma and intrusion, aggression is more likely PTSD arousal than oppositional defiant disorder
  3. 41-year-old man laid off from his job 5 weeks ago tearful, sleeping poorly, cannot focus on job applications still enjoys time with his children; no guilt or thoughts of death energy and appetite normal; no past mood episodes → Adjustment disorder with depressed mood → a non-traumatic stressor 5 weeks ago and fewer than 5 depressive symptoms: adjustment disorder with depressed mood; major depressive disorder needs 5 or more, and persistent depressive disorder needs 2 years
  4. 20-year-old college student whose parents announced their divorce 1 month ago worried and restless; cannot sit through lectures grades slipping; sleeps adequately; eats normally no past anxiety; no substance use; vital signs and examination normal → Adjustment disorder with anxiety → anxiety and impaired function within 3 months of a non-traumatic stressor, short of another disorder: adjustment disorder with anxiety; generalized anxiety needs 6 months or more, and acute stress disorder needs a life-threatening trauma
  5. 33-year-old firefighter treated for PTSD after a fatal building collapse flashbacks and avoidance much improved after CBT and 5 months of sertraline still wakes most nights from vivid dreams of the collapse blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg; drinks rarely → Add prazosin at bedtime → PTSD better on CBT and an SSRI but nightmares persist: add prazosin, an alpha-1 blocker, titrated for blood pressure; a benzodiazepine does not help the nightmares, and switching a working SSRI could worsen other PTSD symptoms
  6. 50-year-old woman found by police at a bus station 300 miles from home cannot give her name, address or job; attention and reasoning intact her son died suddenly 2 days earlier urine toxicology negative; neurologic examination normal → Dissociative amnesia with fugue → lost identity and personal history after a stressor, with travel, intact cognition and no substance or neurologic cause: dissociative amnesia with fugue; transient global amnesia keeps identity, and dissociative identity disorder needs 2 or more identities
  7. 24-year-old graduate student with months of recurrent episodes of feeling detached says she watches herself from outside, as if in a film knows the feeling is not real; memory for events intact no drug use; neurologic examination normal → Depersonalization/derealization disorder → recurrent detachment from herself with reality testing and memory intact, and no substance or neurologic cause: depersonalization/derealization disorder; intact reality testing argues against psychosis, and intact memory against dissociative amnesia
  8. 28-year-old woman seen 10 days after being sexually assaulted nightmares, startles easily, avoids the street where it happened feels numb and in a fog much of the day no suicidal thoughts; no substance use; examination normal → Trauma-focused CBT → acute stress disorder 10 days after a sexual assault: trauma-focused CBT first, started early to lower the risk of PTSD; drugs are typically not needed, and prazosin is an adjunct for PTSD nightmares that persist on an SSRI
Pairs with Major Depressive Disorder covers a full depressive episode after a loss. Psychosis covers brief psychotic disorder, often after a stressor. Cluster B Personality Disorders covers borderline personality and childhood trauma. Cluster C Personality Disorders covers dependent personality.
Transferable rule

After a trauma or stressor, ask what it was and how long since: a life-threatening trauma 3 days to 1 month after the trauma is acute stress disorder and over 1 month is PTSD; any other stressor, with symptoms short of another disorder, is adjustment disorder.
